title: Session 2 — Participant 27 User + Claude Behavior Graphs
goal: TURN SESSION 1'S PROVEN PLATE DESIGN INTO A FINISHED, REPRODUCIBLE TERRAIN CROSS-SECTION ATLAS: RENDER THE FULL MULTI-PAGE DRAFT, QA IT AGAINST THE WRITTEN CRITERIA, RE-IMPLEMENT THE ACCEPTED DESIGN NATIVELY AS A QGIS PRINT LAYOUT DRIVEN BY ATLAS, AND PACKAGE THE REPRODUCIBILITY BUNDLE (GPKG, SURVEY FIELD BOOK, STYLE FILES, PROJECT TEMPLATE, METADATA) SO A THIRD PARTY CAN REGENERATE THE PDF WITHOUT THE PARTICIPANT
context:
Session 1 produced one finished page and proved it was the right page: a map of one stretch of river with its terrain slices drawn underneath, laid out with all the reference information a professional map must carry. Session 2 turns that one page into the whole document, and then rebuilds it a second time inside the mapping software itself.

The rebuild is the interesting part. The first version was drawn by a plotting library — fast and flexible, but it lives in a script and only I can regenerate it. The second version lives in a QGIS project file, where the page is a template and the software walks the river automatically, producing one page per stretch. That version is the one a colleague can open, adjust, and re-run. Getting the two to look the same is genuinely difficult: two different rendering engines, two separate descriptions of the same colours and line weights, and no automatic check that they agree. The session ends by packaging everything with a written record of where they still diverge and why.

session_goal_achievement.Why or why not: The core objective was reached: the full multi-page atlas was rendered, QA'd and signed off, the design was re-implemented natively in QGIS, and the Atlas was wired and exported over the reach layer. What did not happen inside the session was Step 5 — consolidating everything into a delivery folder with a README, metadata record and verification note. The session ran past its 60-minute budget, though by less than Session 1 did, so the plan's decision to front-load the native QGIS work helped. The remaining gap is packaging rather than analysis: every substantive artefact the atlas depends on exists and is correct, but the reproducibility bundle that lets someone else regenerate it unaided has not been assembled. There is also one design-level caveat carried out of Step 4, recorded there: the cross-sections in the QGIS layout are placed as pre-rendered SVG images rather than being drawn by QGIS's built-in elevation profile tool, which works and reproduces the approved plate but is not the ideal native implementation.

nodes.label: Produce a proposed execution plan

nodes.label: Self-audit the plan against the actual Session 1 record
nodes.detail: Re-reads its own proposal against what Session 1 actually produced and reports 8 discrepancies, 4 of which 'would have cost time on the clock': (A1) Step 1.1 inventories a GPKG that doesn't work — Session 1's own MANIFEST calls it 'unreliable on this volume'; adds a real rebuild step; (A2) the cost model is backwards — the composer never touches the 65.7GB ortho, it reads a 0.5m/px .npy already in memory, so QGIS against the full orthomosaic (not the Python render) is the real bottleneck; moves the gdaladdo probe to start at minute 0; (A3) the spec amendment was scheduled around minute 20, late enough that QA round 1 would check plates against a still-stale 40m-spacing spec — moved earlier; (A5) the QGIS Atlas frames on the reach centreline while the spec frames on the transect bounding box, a ~200m gap that would otherwise surface later looking like a renderer bug instead of an extent bug — fixed by precomputing extents onto the reaches layer during the GPKG rebuild. Also corrects two factual mis-statements (geomorphology is vector not raster; reach ordering is confluence-driven, not hydrological), resolves several open placeholders directly from the data (R12 as the 17-transect worst-case cost-timing probe; R08 high-relief/R09 low-relief as the VE-policy test pair; R14 flagged as a QA-20 spike-vs-terrain target), and writes the reconciled plan to S2_prompt_script_v2.md

nodes.label: Review the reconciled plan and authorize execution

nodes.label: Kick off the pyramid build, then rebuild the GPKG and self-correct its own audit
nodes.detail: Starts the gdaladdo overview build in the background while running the inventory in parallel. Mid-rebuild, discovers real GDAL 3.12.4 is available via pyogrio and that project.gpkg actually opens cleanly for reading — explicitly stating it needs 'to correct my own audit before going further.' The write side still hits the exact same sandbox mount bug Session 1 hit (SQLite can't create or reliably read a table there), so it patches the write path by building on local disk and byte-copying the finished file across. Delivers a clean rebuilt project.gpkg — 3 layers (17 reaches/118 transects/11,918 profile points), EPSG:9377 throughout, R01's stored extent recomputing to a delta of 0.000000000m — then surfaces two findings needing a decision before continuing: the nice-round scale series (ceiling 1:10,000) doesn't cover R06 or R12, whose fallback would print an ugly non-round scale; and the spec's framing prose disagrees with what the actual composition code does (reach centreline + transects, not transect bbox alone) — recommends following the code, since that's what produced the approved plate

nodes.label: Resolve the scale-series and framing decisions
nodes.detail: Chooses to extend the nice-scale series with 12500/15000/20000 rather than keep the round-to-500 fallback; confirms following the code's framing behavior and having it written into spec v1.1 rather than the original prose

nodes.label: Amend the spec, correct a scale-series mistake, render the atlas, and deliver the Step 1 package
nodes.detail: Applies all 14 spec edits, then catches and corrects its own just-given answer: R06 and R12 don't both land on 1:12,500 after all — R12 actually needs 1:15,000 (1,690m of window width against 12,500's 1,625m) — and fixes the series before rendering. Regenerates extents against the corrected scale series, patches the composition function to render all 17 reaches into a single PDF via local disk rather than the sandbox mount. Reports its own-initiative changes (moving a hardcoded nodata string into the token file, closing a QA-15 violation), flags one thing for the user's Step 2 critique list (on R09 six of seven tiles hit the 1.80m relief clamp), notes two recurring sandbox mount limitations, and delivers the finished atlas_terrain_profiles_v1.pdf, cartographic_spec.md, style_tokens.json and proof_R09.png

nodes.label: Run the QA sweep and flag one real judgement call

Resolves its own earlier R14 concern cleanly by inspecting both flagged tiles' elevation profiles directly (continuous monotonic slope, not an unfiltered spike). Surfaces the one substantive judgement call: 43 of 118 tiles (36%) sit against the 1.80m relief clamp — R05 is 7 of 8, R09 is 6 of 7, R16 is 7 of 8 — where the annotated vertical-exaggeration value describes the clamp rather than the actual terrain, making near-flat ground look dramatic

nodes.label: Resolve the relief-clamp decision

nodes.label: Apply the agreed fix and re-render

Re-renders the full atlas as v2 in one pass — 17/17 pages, 0 failures, 73 seconds — and reports explicitly that it made no further changes beyond the mechanics of the agreed fix

Step 3.step_name: Generate QML symbology and build the QGIS Print Layout

The script runs on my machine, not in Cowork's sandbox, so it must be written defensively and report progress per stage — expect one or two traceback round-trips and treat them as part of the budget.

Explains its own design choices unprompted: fonts resolve to DejaVu Serif/Sans since those ship with QGIS; one stage specifically checks whether the orthomosaic's .ovr pyramid exists yet and names a fallback if not, rather than let a stalled gdaladdo silently surface as a blank 17-page export later; flags that copying the 66GB of Session 1 raster assets into the delivery tree is a packaging-time decision it won't make unasked. Finds the file is 0 bytes on disk, timestamped 11:01 — after its own verification at 10:48 had reported 32/32 checks passing. Admits the gap directly: that read-back was hitting the sandbox's cache, so it validated a file that never durably landed, and copying the file back through the same layer that wrote it 'proves nothing.' Step 1.step_name: Restore session state and render the full draft atlas
Step 1.step_action: Re-establish Cowork's context from the Session 1 artefacts rather than re-explaining them: point it at the spec, the style tokens, the GPKG and the composition script, and have it confirm what it finds (layer counts, transect count, reach IDs, the naming convention). Then loop the Session 1 composition function over every reach to produce the full draft PDF, plus the standalone profile grid images that Step 4 will need. Confirm the page count is what the spec expects before rendering, not after.
Step 1.input: cartographic_spec.md, style_tokens.json, project.gpkg, composition script, reference plate PNG.
Step 1.tools: Free: Python (matplotlib, rasterio, geopandas), QGIS 3.x. Paid: Claude Pro (Cowork).
rubrics: (Carried from S1 v1 Step 5; now assessable across the whole atlas.)
Every mandatory layout element is present and genuinely populated, no placeholder text, no empty locator map.
All profiles share the same x-extent, and the agreed vertical exaggeration policy is applied identically across every plate.
Map window framing follows the spec: the reach is fully contained, zoom is consistent between pages, and transect lines are legible over the orthomosaic.
The scale bar corresponds to true ground distance and the north arrow reflects the actual projection, both verified, not decorative.
The PDF is print-ready at the target page size: no text overlap, no clipped elements, labels legible at 100%.

ratings.output_quality_reason: Two things had to work here, and both did. First, Cowork picked the project back up from the Session 1 artefacts alone (the spec, the style tokens, the GPKG and the composition script) and confirmed what it found rather than asking me to re-explain the project. That mattered more than it sounds: re-establishing context is where a second session usually loses its first fifteen minutes, and it did not. Second, the composition function scaled from the single proven plate to the whole reach set without breaking. Every mandatory layout element is present and genuinely populated on every page — no placeholder text, no empty locator map. The shared x-extent and the agreed vertical exaggeration policy are applied identically across all plates, which is the clause that could not be tested in Session 1 and is the real risk when going from one page to many. Framing and zoom stay consistent between pages, with the reach fully contained and transect lines legible over the orthomosaic throughout. Scale bar and north arrow were verified against true ground distance and the actual projection. The PDF is print-ready at the target page size with no text overlapping or clipping elements. Rated 5 because the scale-up exposed nothing.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: Both declared outputs were produced (atlas_terrain_profiles_v1.pdf and a profile_<reach_id>.png for every reach) and both were correct without correction rounds. The restore-from-artefacts approach worked as designed, which validates the decision in Session 1 to write the spec and style tokens as machine-readable files rather than leaving criteria in conversation. The effort saving was real but not maximal, because batch rendering is largely mechanical once the composition function is right; the genuine contribution was the context restoration and the verification of layer counts and transect totals before rendering anything.

rubrics: (Carried verbatim from S1 v1 Step 6.)
Every criticism I raise is either addressed in the next revision or explicitly declined with a stated reason; none is quietly ignored.
Fixes do not regress elements I had already accepted in the previous round.
Two rounds are enough to reach a plate I would sign off on and send to a client.

ratings.output_quality_reason: The revision round did exactly what a revision round should. Every criticism I raised was either addressed in the next version or explicitly declined with a reason given (nothing was quietly dropped, which is the failure mode that makes iterative work with an assistant expensive. The fixes did not regress anything I had already accepted in the previous state, so I did not have to re-check work I had already signed off. Design decisions taken during the iteration were written back into cartographic_spec.md and style_tokens.json, so the specification and the output did not drift apart) the spec still describes the atlas that exists. The agent was clear about which changes I had asked for and which it had chosen to make on its own initiative, which is what let me approve quickly instead of auditing every difference. atlas_terrain_profiles_v2.pdf is a plate I sign off and send to a client.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: A signed-off atlas came out of one revision round, with the spec and style tokens updated to match. This was the most efficient step of the session. Cartographic critique is hard to communicate (it is largely judgement about proportion, density and legibility) and the agent turned my comments into the right changes without me having to specify implementation. Keeping the spec synchronised with the output as part of the same round, rather than as a separate cleanup task I would have deferred and probably skipped, is the part I valued most: it is what makes the Session 1 specification still trustworthy at the end of Session 2.

Step 3.step_name: Generate QML symbology and build the QGIS Print Layout
Step 3.step_action: Cowork generates the QML style files for drainage, transects, reaches and geomorphology from the same style_tokens.json that drove the matplotlib plates, then writes a PyQGIS script that I paste into the QGIS Python console to load the layers in spec draw order, apply the styles, and author the Print Layout: map item, picture item for the profile grid, scale bar, north arrow, locator inset map, and label items for CRS, project name, attribution, location and sheet number. The script runs on my machine, not in Cowork's sandbox, so it must be written defensively and report progress per stage — expect one or two traceback round-trips and treat them as part of the budget.
Step 3.input: style_tokens.json; project.gpkg; rasters; accepted plate design.
Step 3.output: styles/*.qml; QGIS project with a Print Layout matching the approved plate.
Step 3.tools: Free: QGIS 3.x (Python console). Paid: Claude Pro (Cowork).
rubrics: (31, 32, 34 carried from S1 v1 Step 7; 41–42 new.)
The script runs in the QGIS Python console with at most two correction cycles, and each traceback I paste back is diagnosed correctly on the first attempt.
The .qgz opens cleanly on a fresh QGIS start with every layer path resolving — no broken links, no missing styles.
QML styles are generated from the same style_tokens.json used in the Python composition, so the QGIS rendering matches the approved plate rather than reinventing the symbology.
Every QML loads without warnings and applies to its layer on first attempt, with layer draw order matching the spec rather than GPKG order.

The Print Layout reproduces the approved plate anatomy at the correct page size — map item, profile picture frame, scale bar, north arrow, locator inset and every label item present at the specified position and relative size.

ratings.output_quality_reason:
The end state is correct and usable, but this was the roughest step of the session and the one that consumed the overrun. What worked cleanly: the .qgz opens on a fresh QGIS start with every layer path resolving (no broken links, no missing styles) and the QML files were genuinely generated from the same style_tokens.json that drove the matplotlib composition, so the QGIS rendering follows the approved symbology instead of reinventing it. That single-source-of-truth decision is what kept the two renderers comparable at all.
Three things fell short. The PyQGIS script needed more than the two correction cycles the rubric allows; I pasted several tracebacks back, and while each was diagnosed sensibly, the loop ran longer than budgeted. The QML files did not all load silently and cleanly on first application; I had to resolve warnings and correct layer draw order, which had followed GPKG order rather than the order the spec defines. And the Print Layout could not be built in the same pass as the project: it required a separate script from the one that creates the .qgz, loads the data layers and applies the QML styles. That split is workable and I kept both scripts, but it means the "one script builds the project" outcome I was aiming for was not achieved, and reproducing the project now means running two scripts in the right order; which is exactly the kind of undocumented sequencing that Step 5 was meant to capture and did not get to.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: The task was completed (QML styles exist, are token-derived, and the Print Layout matches the approved plate) but it took visible debugging to get there. PyQGIS is an awkward API to write blind, without a live QGIS session to introspect, and that shows in the number of correction cycles. What made the loop tolerable was the quality of the diagnosis: each traceback I pasted was read correctly and produced a targeted fix rather than a speculative rewrite, and I never lost the thread of what the script was doing. The effort saving is still clearly positive (authoring QML by hand and building a Print Layout item by item in the GUI would have taken considerably longer than the debugging did) but it is the least efficient step of the session.

Step 4.step_name: Wire the Atlas, export, and reconcile against the approved plate
Step 4.step_action: Configure the Atlas against the reaches layer: coverage, page ordering, map item following the Atlas feature with the spec's framing and buffer, and the picture item resolving profile images by expression from reach_id. Export to PDF, then reconcile against the plate approved in Step 2 -- for every visible difference, determine whether it is a QML value disagreeing with the style tokens (fix it) or a genuine renderer difference between matplotlib and QGIS (document it). This reconciliation is the substantive test of R-07 and should not be rushed to save the packaging step.
Step 4.input: QGIS project from Step 3; profile images; approved plate.
Step 4.output: atlas_template.qgz; atlas_qgis.pdf; list of classified divergences.
Step 4.tools: Free: QGIS 3.x (Print Layout, Atlas, Python console). Paid: Claude Pro (Cowork).
rubrics: (33, 35 carried from S1 v1 Step 7; 43–45 new.)
The Atlas iterates over the reach layer and the profile image resolves by expression on every page, including the first and last.
The Atlas-exported PDF is visually equivalent to the design approved in Step 2, and any unavoidable divergence is reported to me rather than left for me to discover.
The Atlas map item follows each reach with the spec's framing and buffer — no page where the reach is clipped, off-centre, or rendered at an inconsistent zoom.
Page count and page order match the reach layer exactly, with sheet numbering correct on every page.
Each divergence from the approved plate is classified as either a style-token mismatch (and fixed) or a genuine renderer difference (and documented), rather than dismissed or silently absorbed.

ratings.output_quality_reason:
The Atlas works end to end, which was the goal of the whole migration. It iterates over the reach layer and the profile image resolves by expression on every page, including the first and last; the classic Atlas failure is an expression that works on page one and silently breaks on the edges, and that did not happen. Page count and page order match the reach layer exactly, with sheet numbering correct throughout. Divergences from the approved plate were properly classified as either style-token mismatches, which were fixed, or genuine renderer differences between matplotlib and QGIS, which were documented rather than dismissed. I rated the output 4 because atlas_template.qgz and atlas_qgis.pdf are the deliverables I needed and they are sound.
Two qualifications. Map framing did not hold on every page: some reaches came out clipped or off-centre relative to the spec's buffer rule, and those pages needed correction. And not every divergence from the approved design was reported to me upfront; I found some myself when comparing the two PDFs side by side, which is the opposite of the arrangement I wanted, where the agent surfaces differences rather than leaving me to discover them.
Additional observation on the profile implementation. The cross-section plots in the layout are the SVG profiles extracted in Step 1, inserted as SVG picture items and wired per page by expression from reach_id. Every page resolves its correct profile, so the mechanism is sound and the output is right. But the ideal native implementation would have used QGIS's built-in elevation profile tool to recreate the cross-sections inside the project, rather than importing images generated by an external Python script. As built, the QGIS project is not fully self-contained: regenerating the profiles still depends on the Python pipeline. This is a real limitation of the migration, and I am recording it here rather than letting it pass as equivalent. It sits closest to Rubric 35; the export is visually equivalent to the approved design, but by a different mechanism than a native QGIS implementation implies.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: A working, exportable QGIS Atlas exists and produces the atlas PDF, which is what the step had to deliver. The collaboration was less comfortable than in earlier steps. Atlas configuration involves a lot of interacting specifics (coverage layer, page ordering, map item behaviour, expression-driven picture resolution, framing buffer) and I had to correct the agent's reading of what I wanted more than once, which is why I marked understanding lower here. It adapted precisely each time, and I retained full control of the design decisions throughout. The reconciliation against the approved plate is where I contributed most: I would have preferred divergences surfaced to me systematically rather than discovering some by comparison, and the SVG-versus-native-profile question is one I had to raise rather than being offered as a trade-off up front.

ratings.output_quality_reason:
No numeric rating, because this step was never opened during the recorded session and there is therefore no in-session output to rate. The rubrics below are still assessable, because the deliverables Step 5 was meant to consolidate all exist and are correct from Steps 1–4, and the delivery folder has since been assembled. Rating the step numerically would mean scoring work the agent was never asked to do; assessing the rubrics against the accumulated outputs is the honest way to report where the deliverable actually stands.
Deferring the step was a scoping decision as much as a time-budget one. The session did run past its 60-minute budget, though by less than Session 1 did. But the deliberate part was this: by the end of Step 4 the hard problem was solved. The automation script had done the difficult work (the QGIS project, the styles, the Print Layout and the working Atlas all existed) and what remained in Step 5 was consolidation of outputs that were already compliant from the preceding steps. I also expected the QGIS project to need some manual editing before it was final, which made it a poor moment to freeze a delivery bundle around it. Packaging a project I still intended to touch would have produced a folder I would immediately have had to rebuild. Given a choice between spending the remaining session time on packaging and stopping at a completed, verified Atlas, stopping was the better use of the recording.

goal_achievement.Why or why not: There is no interaction to evaluate. The step was never opened with the agent; not attempted and abandoned, but deliberately not started, for the scoping reasons given above. The agent's contribution to the state of this deliverable is real but sits entirely in Steps 1–4, where it produced the artefacts that make the package compliant, and it is already scored there. Rating collaboration here would double-count that work against an interaction that did not take place.
